questions.q: Which gestational weeks span the embryonic period (period of organogenesis), during which all major internal and external organ systems are established and susceptibility to structural teratogens is highest?
questions.explain: The embryonic period extends from the beginning of week 4 to the end of week 8 post-fertilization; by the end of week 8, all major organ systems have begun developing and the embryo has a distinctly human appearance.

open.q: Which gestational weeks constitute the embryonic period of organogenesis?

questions.q: From which embryonic germ layer do the central nervous system, epidermis of the skin, hair, nails, enamel of teeth, and adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary) originate?
questions.explain: Ectoderm divides into neuroectoderm (CNS, retina, neurohypophysis, pineal gland), neural crest, and surface ectoderm (epidermis, skin appendages, lens, inner ear, enamel, and Rathke pouch/adenohypophysis).

open.q: Which primary germ layer gives rise to the central nervous system, epidermis, and tooth enamel?

questions.q: In which anatomical region does fusion of the neural folds begin during week 4, and on which days do the cranial (anterior) and caudal (posterior) neuropores normally close?
options: Fusion begins in the cervical region; the cranial neuropore closes around day 25 and the caudal around days 27–28
Fusion begins in the lumbosacral region; both neuropores close by day 21
Fusion begins in the forebrain; both neuropores close simultaneously on day 22
Fusion begins in the thoracic region; neuropores close after week 5
questions.explain: Neural tube fusion starts in the future cervical region (somite 5) on day 21–22 and zips bidirectionally; the cranial neuropore closes around day 25 and the caudal neuropore closes 2 to 3 days later (day 27–28).

open.q: On approximately which days after fertilization do the cranial and caudal neuropores close respectively?

questions.q: A newborn presents with a midline lumbar cystic sac protruding through unfused vertebral arches containing both meninges and spinal cord tissue (myelomeningocele), accompanied by lower-limb paralysis. Failure of which embryological event directly causes this defect?
options: Closure of the caudal neuropore during week 4
Closure of the cranial neuropore during week 4
questions.explain: Failure of the caudal neuropore to close by day 27–28 results in lumbosacral spina bifida cystica (meningocele or myelomeningocele), whereas failure of cranial neuropore closure causes anencephaly.

open.q: Failure of which embryonic opening to close during week 4 results in spina bifida cystica (myelomeningocele)?

questions.q: Which of the following structures is derived from neural crest cells rather than surface ectoderm or endoderm?
options: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, Schwann cells, and melanocytes
Adrenal cortex, hepatocytes, and renal tubules
Enamel of teeth, lens of the eye, and epidermis
Epithelial lining of the trachea and urinary bladder
questions.explain: Neural crest derivatives include dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, odontoblasts, parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid, and aorticopulmonary septum.

open.q: Name three structures in the human body derived from neural crest cells.
accept: dorsal root ganglia, Schwann cells, and melanocytes
melanocytes, adrenal medulla, and autonomic ganglia

questions.q: Which two thickened surface ectodermal placodes on the developing head invaginate during weeks 4 to 5 to form the lens of the eye and the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear?
questions.explain: Surface ectoderm thickens into bilateral lens placodes (invaginating into lens vesicles) and otic placodes (invaginating into otic vesicles/otocysts that form the inner ear).

open.q: Name the surface ectodermal thickening that invaginates to form the otic vesicle (primordium of the inner ear).

questions.q: Into which three functional subdivisions does each somite (derived from paraxial mesoderm) differentiate during week 4?
questions.explain: Each somite differentiates ventromedially into the sclerotome (vertebrae and ribs) and dorsolaterally into the dermomyotome, which splits into the myotome (skeletal muscles) and dermatome (dermis of the dorsal skin).

open.q: List the three subdivisions into which each somite differentiates during the fourth week.

questions.q: Which somite subdivision migrates medially around the neural tube and notochord to form the vertebral column and ribs?
questions.explain: Ventromedial sclerotome cells undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and surround the notochord and neural tube; resegmentation of adjacent sclerotome halves forms each definitive vertebral body.

open.q: Which part of a somite gives rise to the vertebrae and ribs?

questions.q: Into which two divisions does each somitic myotome split to form the intrinsic deep back muscles versus the limb and anterolateral body wall muscles?
questions.explain: Each myotome splits into a small dorsal epimere (innervated by dorsal primary rami, forming epaxial intrinsic back muscles) and a larger ventral hypomere (innervated by ventral primary rami, forming hypaxial body wall and limb muscles).

open.q: Name the dorsal and ventral divisions of the myotome that form the epaxial and hypaxial skeletal muscles respectively.

questions.q: Which embryonic mesodermal column gives rise to the kidneys, ureters, gonads, and their genital duct systems?
questions.explain: Intermediate mesoderm lies between paraxial and lateral plate mesoderm and forms the longitudinal urogenital ridge, giving rise to the pronephros, mesonephros, metanephros, gonads, and mesonephric/paramesonephric ducts.

open.q: Which division of intraembryonic mesoderm gives rise to the urinary and genital systems?

questions.q: When the intraembryonic coelom splits the lateral plate mesoderm into somatic (parietal) and splanchnic (visceral) layers, what do these two layers form respectively?
options: Somatic mesoderm contributes to body wall and parietal serosa; splanchnic mesoderm contributes to visceral serosa and gut/heart tissues
Somatic mesoderm forms vertebrae; splanchnic mesoderm forms spinal cord
Somatic mesoderm forms gut mucosa; splanchnic mesoderm forms epidermis
Somatic mesoderm forms kidneys; splanchnic mesoderm forms adrenal medulla
questions.explain: Somatic mesoderm plus overlying ectoderm (somatopleure) forms the lateral/ventral body wall, parietal pleura/pericardium/peritoneum, and limb skeletal elements; splanchnic mesoderm plus endoderm (splanchnopleure) forms the visceral serous layers, myocardium, blood vessels, and gut wall muscle/connective tissue.

open.q: Which layer of lateral plate mesoderm contributes to the myocardium and smooth muscle of the gastrointestinal tract?

questions.q: Which of the following structures is derived from the embryonic endoderm?
options: Gut and respiratory epithelium, bladder lining, and liver and pancreatic parenchyma
Epidermis, lens and central nervous system
questions.explain: Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the primitive gut tube (pharynx to upper anal canal), respiratory tree, tympanic cavity and auditory tube, urinary bladder and urethra, and secretory parenchyma of thyroid, parathyroids, thymus, liver, and pancreas.

open.q: Name three organs or epithelial linings derived from the embryonic endoderm.
accept: gastrointestinal epithelium, respiratory epithelium, and liver parenchyma
lining of gut tube, respiratory tract, and urinary bladder

questions.q: What primary developmental mechanism drives cephalocaudal and lateral embryonic folding during the fourth week?
options: Rapid neural tube and somite growth, together with expansion of the amniotic cavity
Contraction of smooth muscle in the connecting stalk
questions.explain: During week 4, rapid lengthening of the dorsal neural tube and somites causes head and tail folds, while transverse growth of somites and amniotic cavity expansion folds the lateral edges ventrally to incorporate the dorsal yolk sac into the primitive gut tube.

open.q: Which cavity enlarges rapidly during week 4 to surround the folding embryo and obliterate the chorionic cavity?

questions.q: As a consequence of cephalocaudal folding during week 4, where does the cardiogenic area (primordial heart) move relative to the oropharyngeal membrane and septum transversum?
options: The heart moves ventrally and caudally, coming to lie cranial to the septum transversum
Into the dorsal lumbar region behind the notochord
Into the umbilical cord beside the allantois
questions.explain: Head folding swings the cardiogenic field and pericardial coelom ventrally and caudally through ~180 degrees so the heart lies ventral to the foregut and cranial to the septum transversum (primordium of the central tendon of the diaphragm).

open.q: Through approximately how many degrees does head folding swing the cardiogenic area ventrally into the future thorax?

questions.q: Which narrow duct connects the midgut to the definitive yolk sac (umbilical vesicle) after lateral embryonic folding constricts the ventral body wall?
questions.explain: Lateral folding pinches off the dorsal part of the yolk sac as the primitive gut tube, leaving the midgut temporarily connected to the yolk sac via the narrow vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct inside the umbilical cord.

open.q: Name the narrow embryonic channel connecting the midgut to the yolk sac after lateral folding.

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy presents with painless bright-red rectal bleeding; a technetium-99m pertechnetate scan detects ectopic gastric mucosa on the antimesenteric border of the distal ileum (Meckel diverticulum). Failure of obliteration of which embryonic structure accounts for this anomaly?
options: Proximal portion of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct
questions.explain: Persistence of the proximal intra-abdominal segment of the vitelline duct produces Meckel (ileal) diverticulum, which follows the 'rule of 2s' (2% of population, 2 inches long, within 2 feet of ileocecal valve, often containing ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue).

open.q: Persistence of the proximal portion of which embryonic duct causes Meckel diverticulum?

questions.q: A full-term newborn presents with loops of small intestine protruding directly through a small right-sided paraumbilical abdominal wall defect WITHOUT any covering amniotic membrane (gastroschisis). Which defect during week 4 underlies this condition?
options: Incomplete closure/fusion of the right lateral body wall fold during lateral embryonic folding
Failure of physiological midgut herniation to return into the abdomen during week 10
questions.explain: Gastroschisis results from failure of lateral body wall folding (usually right of the midline) during week 4, leaving viscera exposed directly to amniotic fluid with no sac; by contrast, omphalocele is covered by an amnion-peritoneum sac at the umbilicus.

open.q: How does the presence or absence of a covering sac distinguish omphalocele from gastroschisis at birth?
accept: omphalocele is covered by an amniotic sac whereas gastroschisis has no covering sac
omphalocele has a sac; gastroschisis lacks a sac

questions.q: In which developmental sequence do the upper and lower limb buds first appear during week 4?
options: Upper limb buds appear first (around day 24–26), followed 1 to 2 days later by lower limb buds (day 26–28)
Lower limb buds appear a full week before upper limb buds
Both upper and lower limb buds appear simultaneously on day 15
Limb buds do not appear until week 9
questions.explain: Following the craniocaudal gradient of embryonic maturation, upper limb buds emerge opposite somites C5–T2 around day 24–26, and lower limb buds emerge opposite somites L1–S2 about 1 to 2 days later.

open.q: Which pair of limb buds emerges first during the fourth week of development, and by approximately how many days do they precede the other pair?
accept: upper limb buds appear 1 to 2 days before lower limb buds

questions.q: Which thickened band of ectoderm at the distal tip of each growing limb bud secretes fibroblast growth factors (FGF4 and FGF8) to maintain the underlying progress zone and drive proximodistal limb outgrowth?
questions.explain: The apical ectodermal ridge (AER) runs along the distal rim of the limb bud and secretes FGFs that keep underlying mesenchymal cells in the progress zone rapidly proliferating for proximodistal elongation.

open.q: Name the thickened distal ectodermal rim of the limb bud that regulates proximodistal outgrowth via FGF signaling.

questions.q: Which signaling center at the posterior base of the limb bud secretes Sonic hedgehog (SHH) to pattern the anteroposterior (thumb-to-little-finger / preaxial-to-postaxial) axis of the digits?
questions.explain: The zone of polarizing activity (ZPA) is a cluster of mesenchymal cells at the posterior border of the limb bud secreting a morphogen gradient of Sonic hedgehog (SHH); ectopic anterior SHH expression causes mirror-image polydactyly.

open.q: Name the posterior mesenchymal signaling region of the limb bud that secretes Sonic hedgehog (SHH) to establish the anteroposterior digit axis.

questions.q: During week 7 of development, in which opposite directions do the upper and lower limbs rotate about their longitudinal axes?
options: Upper limbs rotate laterally; lower limbs rotate medially
Upper limbs rotate medially; lower limbs rotate laterally
Both limb pairs rotate 180 degrees medially
Neither limb pair rotates during development
questions.explain: During week 7, upper limbs rotate 90° laterally so thumbs point laterally and extensors face posteriorly, whereas lower limbs rotate 90° medially so big toes (halluces) lie medially and knee extensors face anteriorly.

open.q: State the direction and angle of rotation of the upper limbs versus the lower limbs during week 7.
accept: upper limbs rotate 90 degrees laterally and lower limbs rotate 90 degrees medially

questions.q: By what cellular process are the individual fingers and toes sculpted from the paddle-shaped handplates and footplates during weeks 6 to 8?
options: Programmed cell death (apoptosis) in the interdigital necrotic zones
Conversion of interdigital mesenchyme into cartilage
questions.explain: BMP-mediated apoptosis in the interdigital mesenchymal webs eliminates tissue between the digital rays, separating the digits; failure of interdigital apoptosis causes cutaneous syndactyly (webbed fingers or toes).

open.q: Failure of which cellular process in the interdigital webs during weeks 6–8 results in cutaneous syndactyly?

questions.q: During which embryonic week do the pharyngeal arches first become externally visible, the heart begins beating (around day 22), and the neural tube closes?
questions.explain: Week 4 is marked by embryonic folding, closure of both neuropores, onset of heart contractions around day 22, appearance of pharyngeal arches 1–3, and emergence of the upper and lower limb buds.

open.q: In which embryonic week does the primitive heart begin to beat and do the first pharyngeal arches appear externally?

questions.q: Why does physiological umbilical herniation of the rapidly elongating midgut loop into the proximal umbilical cord normally begin during week 6?
options: Rapid midgut growth and enlargement of the liver leave insufficient abdominal space temporarily
The diaphragm is absent until birth
The amniotic cavity compresses the thoracic wall
The neural tube protrudes into the abdomen
questions.explain: During week 6, rapid elongation of the primary intestinal loop combined with massive growth of the liver and mesonephroi forces the midgut to herniate temporarily into the extraembryonic coelom of the umbilical cord until week 10.

open.q: Which two rapidly enlarging abdominal organs leave insufficient room in the embryonic abdomen during week 6, prompting physiological midgut herniation?

questions.q: Which measurement is standardly used on first-trimester ultrasonography to estimate gestational age between weeks 7 and 14?
questions.explain: Crown-rump length (CRL)—the distance from the vertex of the skull to the midpoint between the buttocks—is the most accurate biometric parameter for dating pregnancy in the late embryonic and early fetal periods.

open.q: Name the standard ultrasound measurement from the top of the head to the buttocks used to date embryos and early fetuses.

questions.q: Failure of the two medial nasal processes to merge with each other and form the intermaxillary segment can contribute to which congenital anomaly?
options: Cleft palate caused solely by failure of palatal shelves to elevate
questions.explain: The paired medial nasal processes merge to form the intermaxillary segment, which contributes to the philtrum of the upper lip, the premaxillary part of the maxilla and the primary palate. Failure of their fusion can produce a median cleft of the upper lip.

questions.q: The secondary palate develops mainly from which embryonic structures?
options: Lateral palatine shelves arising from the maxillary prominences
questions.explain: The secondary palate forms from paired lateral palatine shelves (palatal processes) of the maxillary prominences. The shelves elevate above the tongue and fuse with each other, the primary palate and the nasal septum.

questions.q: A child undergoes surgery for an ectopic thymic remnant in the neck. During embryological review, the surgeon explains that the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands normally migrate together from which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.explain: The third pharyngeal pouch forms the thymus from its ventral wing and the inferior parathyroid glands from its dorsal wing. Their shared descent explains why inferior parathyroid glands may be ectopic along the thymic migration pathway. The superior parathyroid glands arise from the fourth pouch.

open.q: Which pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands?
